summary: Defines a YANG module for managing alarms on network devices. It covers keeping a list of alarms, temporarily shelving alarms, sending notifications to management systems, and operations to set an alarm's operator state and handle administrative alarm procedures. It is designed to map onto existing alarm standards.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of a fire alarm panel that lists every bell ringing, lets you mute one for a while, and tells the caretaker. This gives network gear a common way to do that.

subtitle: A standard YANG model that treats an alarm as a state on a resource, with a list, shelving, operator actions and notifications.

tldr.problem: Alarm standards from ITU, 3GPP and ANSI left it unclear how a notification maps onto an alarm, so network devices reported alarms in many incompatible ways.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a YANG module in which an alarm is a state on a resource, identified by the resource, an alarm-type id and an alarm-type qualifier. It adds an alarm list, an inventory of alarm types, shelving, operator and administrative actions, and notifications.
tldr.outcome: A device that implements the module gives management applications one standard alarm interface, and an optional second module maps it to the X.733 alarm standard. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 8632 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2019, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the ietf-alarms and ietf-alarms-x733 YANG modules.

sections.title: Why a Standard Alarm Model
sections.content:
RFC 8632 defines a YANG module for alarm management. Its purpose is a standardized alarm interface for network devices that is easy to plug into management applications. The model can also serve as a northbound alarm interface in the management applications themselves.

The RFC is modest about what alarms can do. Raw alarms from devices do not always show the status of network services or point to the root cause. Still, feeding them to an alarm-management application in a standard format is a starting point for higher-level network assurance. The design draws on experience with alarm standards from ITU (X.733), 3GPP and ANSI (ISA 18.2).
sections.plainLanguage: Every brand of machine used to shout about problems in its own way. This gives them one common way to say what is wrong.

sections.title: Alarms as States on Resources
sections.content:
The core idea is that an alarm is an undesirable state in a resource that requires corrective action. It is a state, not the notification that reports a change in that state. General events and log information are meant to be left out.

An alarm type is a possible unique alarm state for a resource, such as link-alarm. The alarm-type id is a YANG identity, so standards bodies and vendors can define their own types in a hierarchy. A string alarm-type qualifier allows types that are only known at run time, for example a smoke detector wired to a digital input. A server SHOULD keep such dynamic types to a minimum and MUST publish every possible type in the alarm inventory.

An alarm instance is identified by the tuple of resource, alarm-type id and alarm-type qualifier. Notifications for the same tuple update the same alarm, which removes the ambiguity the RFC says X.733 and the 3GPP documents left open. If the resource exists in the data tree, it MUST be named with an instance-identifier holding the full path.
sections.plainLanguage: An alarm is like a light on a dashboard that is either on or off for one specific part. The same part and the same kind of problem always use the same light.

sections.title: Alarm Lifecycles
sections.content:
The model separates three lifecycles. The resource lifecycle is controlled by the device itself: raise, change severity, clear and raise again. The operator lifecycle covers people acting on alarms. The administrative lifecycle covers purging alarms and compressing their history.

Two rules matter. Alarms are not deleted when they are cleared, because deletion is an administrative job done with the purge-alarms action. And operators cannot clear alarms; only the underlying instrumentation can. Operators can close them, meaning they consider the corrective action done.

The severity values are indeterminate, warning, minor, major and critical. Clearance is not a severity but a separate boolean, is-cleared. The operator state of an alarm can be none, ack, shelved or closed, set with the set-operator-state action.

Per-alarm history is kept in a status-change list when the optional alarm-history feature is implemented. By default the list holds 32 entries, and the oldest entry is dropped when it is full. The compress-alarms action deletes all status-change entries except the last one.
sections.plainLanguage: The machine turns an alarm on and off by itself. A person can say "I saw it" or "I fixed it", but only the machine can switch the light off.

sections.title: The Alarm Data Model
sections.content:
The alarm list and the alarm inventory MUST be implemented, along with the notifications. The rest is controlled by YANG features: operator-actions, alarm-shelving, alarm-history, alarm-summary, alarm-profile and severity-assignment.

  • Control: configuration for how many status changes to keep and which changes trigger notifications (all changes, only raise and clear, or only those crossing a severity level).
  • Alarm inventory: every alarm type the system may raise, so operators can prepare procedures in advance.
  • Summary: counts per severity, such as cleared, closed and not cleared, plus a flag showing whether shelves are active.
  • Alarm list: the current composite state of each alarm. It can also carry hints such as impacted resources, root-cause resources and related alarms.
  • Alarm profiles: configuration that overrides the system-default severity levels for a type of alarm.

The principle is to limit the number of alarms. If a full disk affects a database, the recommendation is one alarm on the disk partition, with the database listed as an impacted resource, rather than separate alarms for each.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a big list of every light that is on, a list of every light the machine could ever have, and a small scoreboard that counts them by how serious they are.

sections.title: Shelving and Notifications
sections.content:
Alarm shelving blocks alarms that match criteria such as a resource or alarm type. Matching alarms MUST appear in the shelved-alarm list and non-matching alarms in the main alarm list. The server sends no notifications for shelved alarms, though the shelved list is still updated. Shelving is done by editing the shelf configuration, not on individual alarms. It is optional because matching alarms against shelves may cost processing resources.

The model has a general notification for alarm-state changes, another reporting that an operator changed an alarm's operator state, and one telling the management application that the alarm inventory changed, for instance when a new card is inserted.
sections.plainLanguage: Shelving is like putting a noisy toy in a cupboard. It is still there, but it stops bothering you until you take it out again.

sections.title: Hardware Module and X.733 Mapping
sections.content:
The RFC relates its model to the ietf-hardware module from RFC 8348, whose alarm-state is only a summary of severities active on a hardware component. For example, no bit set in that field corresponds to an alarm being cleared, and the under-repair bit corresponds to an operator having acknowledged the alarm.

A second module, ietf-alarms-x733, augments the inventory, the alarm lists and the notification with X.733 and X.736 parameters. A management application can also configure how alarm types map to the X.733 event-type and probable-cause parameters. Keeping this in a separate module keeps the core model small.
sections.plainLanguage: Some older control rooms use a different alarm language. A second, optional dictionary translates between the new words and the old ones.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF. Access can be restricted per user with the NETCONF Access Control Model. The RFC points out that the alarm list itself is sensitive, because it gives an attacker an authoritative picture of the broken state of the network.

Writable nodes that need protection include notify-status-changes, the shelf list and the severity assignment profile. Misuse could suppress notifications, hide alarms or downgrade severities. The purge-alarms and set-operator-state actions are also sensitive, since they can delete alarms or cause them to be ignored.

IANA registered two XML namespace URIs and two YANG modules, ietf-alarms and ietf-alarms-x733.
sections.plainLanguage: A list of what is broken is a map for burglars, and being able to mute alarms is powerful. So only trusted people should be allowed to look or press the buttons.
